power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.466", "p=0.690"), Sentence = c("CD68 did not differentiate PsA from seropositive RA (AUC 0.57, 95% CI 0.38-0.74, p=0.466) (Figure 2f).", "Integrating treatment history with pathotype assignments revealed that the pauci-immune pathotype was predominantly identified in treatment-experienced patients (those receiving csDMARDs or b/tsDMARDs; n=7/8), with one treatment-naïve patient assigned this pathotype (Figures 4b-f), although the overall distribution of pathotypes did not differ significantly by treatment (chi-squared p=0.690)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Synovial inflammation in psoriatic arthritis (PsA) lacks a validated histological classification framework.

Current approaches apply rheumatoid arthritis (RA) synovial pathotypes to PsA, which overlooks immunobiological differences between the diseases and limits the predictive power of tissue stratification.
We aimed to define data-driven, PsA-specific synovial pathotypes to facilitate tissue-driven precision medicine.

In this cross-sectional study, ultrasound-guided synovial biopsies were obtained from 61 patients with PsA (n=22), seropositive RA (n=23), seronegative RA (n=10), and other inflammatory arthritides (n=6).
Sections underwent multi-modal staining, including H&E, picrosirius red, and immunohistochemistry for CD3, CD20, CD68, CD138, and CD31.

text.text: Whole-slide digital image analysis and automated pixel classifiers quantified cellular and stromal metrics.
Unsupervised hierarchical clustering identified intrinsic PsA pathotypes, which were correlated with clinical disease activity, radiographic osteoarthritis (OA), and longitudinal treatment responses.

While a subset of PsA patients shared an inflammatory signature with seropositive RA, unsupervised clustering of the PsA cohort revealed three distinct, novel pathotypes: 'Dense Myeloid' (macrophagedriven), 'Fibro-Stromal' (fibrosis and pauci-immune), and 'Angio-Lymphoid' (hypervascular with significant CD138 + plasma cell infiltration).
Pathotypes were independent of treatment and concurrent radiographic knee OA.
The Fibro-Stromal pathotype correlated with significantly higher cutaneous psoriasis severity.

Longitudinally, patients with the Fibro-Stromal pathotype exhibited a trend toward lower treatment response (44%) following standard interventions (methotrexate or TNF inhibitors) compared to the Dense Myeloid (50%) and Angio-Lymphoid (80%) pathotypes.
We present the first computationally derived synovial pathotypes specific to PsA, revealing distinct plasma cell and fibrotic architectures not captured by RA-centric models.

To enable clinical translation, we distilled these findings into a pragmatic, four-marker diagnostic decision tree (CD31, CD68, CD138, and picrosirius red) designed for routine histopathology workflows, providing a staging ground for biomarker-stratified clinical trials in PsA.

The potential clinical utility of tissue-based patient stratification is well established in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), where baseline synovial pathotypes (lympho-myeloid, diffuse-myeloid, and pauciimmune) have guided targeted biologic therapy in landmark precision medicine trials.

However, psoriatic arthritis (PsA) exhibits a fundamentally distinct synovial microenvironment, characterised by unique vascular architecture, altered stromal fibroblast phenotypes, and distinct immune infiltrates intertwined with the IL-23/IL-17 cytokine axis.
Consequently, attempting to classify PsA synovial tissue using established RA-derived scoring systems risks misrepresenting intrinsic disease biology.

There is currently no validated, disease-specific histological classification system for PsA, which forces therapeutic decision-making to rely on an empirical, trial-and-error approach rather than underlying target tissue pathobiology.
To our knowledge, this is the first study to define data-driven, computationally derived synovial pathotypes entirely specific to PsA.

By leveraging multi-modal digital pathology and unsupervised machine learning, we deconstructed the PsA synovium into three biologically distinct pathotypes: Dense Myeloid, Fibro-Stromal, and Angio-Lymphoid.
We demonstrated that the highly inflammatory PsA microenvironment is distinctly driven by CD138 + plasma cells rather than the CD20 + B cells typically observed in RA.

Furthermore, we identified a striking tissue-level divergence: patients with the highly fibrotic, pauci-immune Fibro-Stromal pathotype exhibited the most severe cutaneous psoriasis and demonstrated a trend toward higher failure rates on standard therapies, independent of concurrent osteoarthritis.
Crucially, we translated these high-dimensional computational findings into a pragmatic, four-marker diagnostic decision tree (incorporating CD31, CD68, CD138, and picrosirius red).
This study establishes that PsA synovial pathology requires a dedicated, disease-specific classification framework.
The proposed diagnostic decision tree can be integrated into routine clinical histopathology workflows without the immediate need for advanced spatial or single-cell transcriptomics.

Furthermore, the correlation between the Fibro-Stromal pathotype, severe skin disease, and poor joint response to standard therapies provides a biological rationale for stratifying this specific subgroup towards early IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor intervention alongside conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs.

Ultimately, these novel PsA pathotypes provide the vital staging ground required to design and execute biomarker-stratified, tissue-driven clinical trials, paving the way for precision medicine in PsA.

text.text: This highlights an urgent, unmet need to develop data-driven synovial pathotypes specific to PsA.

To address this gap, this study aimed to define clinically meaningful, data-driven PsA synovial pathotypes using multi-modal histology and machine learning, and to subsequently construct a clinically translatable diagnostic decision tree.

Moving beyond traditional, subjective, and semi-quantitative manual scoring, we leveraged whole-slide digital pathology to extract objective cellular and stromal metrics from the synovial microenvironment.

By applying unsupervised machine learning techniques to these datasets, we sought to uncover intrinsic, biologically meaningful histological subgroups within PsA and contrast their features with seropositive and seronegative RA.
Finally, to ensure clinical utility, we distilled these computationally derived signatures into a simplified, accessible immunohistochemistry (IHC) scoring tool.

Designed for seamless implementation into routine pathology workflows, this novel, disease-specific classification system provides the critical framework required to facilitate future biomarker-stratified, tissue-driven clinical trials in PsA.

This cross-sectional, observational study evaluated inflamed synovial tissue from patients with PsA (fulfilling CASPAR criteria) and seropositive (defined strictly by anti-citrullinated protein antibody [ACPA] positivity, independent of rheumatoid factor status) or seronegative (ACPA negative, independent of rheumatoid factor status) RA (fulfilling 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria).

Following informed written consent, patients with ultrasound-detected joint inflammation (grey-scale ≥2 and power Doppler ≥1) underwent ultrasound-guided, minimally invasive synovial needle core biopsy.
The anatomical site of the biopsied joint was recorded for all patients.
Baseline clinical metrics including psoriasis body surface area (BSA), joint counts, global assessments, and acute phase reactants were captured at the time of biopsy.

To account for potential confounding from secondary degenerative changes, particularly given the high proportion of knee biopsies, concurrent radiographic osteoarthritis (OA) severity at the biopsied joint was evaluated from pre-biopsy imaging and graded as none, mild, moderate, or severe. 37 Additionally, longitudinal clinical trajectories were tracked from the date of biopsy to the most recent clinical follow-up to evaluate post-biopsy treatment changes and therapeutic responses.

text.text: Synovial biopsy cores were formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded (FFPE).
To comprehensively capture synovial inflammation, stromal fibrosis, and vascularity, serial 5µm sections underwent a multi-modal staining strategy.
General morphological assessment was performed using Haematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) staining.

text.text: Picrosirius red with a fast green counterstain was utilised to specifically identify and quantify the collagenous extracellular matrix.

The immune and vascular microenvironments were characterised via automated immunohistochemistry (IHC) using a validated panel of lineage markers: CD3 (T cells), CD20 (B cells), CD68 (macrophages), CD138 (plasma cells), and CD31 (endothelial cells).
High-resolution whole-slide images were analysed in a blinded manner using QuPath software (v0.6.0).
Standardised Krenn synovitis scores and digital cellularity (cells/mm 2 ) were derived from H&E sections.

To identify novel, data-driven synovial pathotypes in PsA, unsupervised agglomerative hierarchical clustering (Ward's linkage, Euclidean distance) was employed.
An input matrix was constructed incorporating cellularity, fibrosis, vascularity, and the four quantitative IHC metrics.

The complete cohort and the lymphomyeloid subset were clustered using k-means clustering to explore histological overlap between diagnoses, with elbow plots and silhouette scores used to evaluate the number of clusters.

For PsA, three clusters were selected because three pathotypes were more informative than two or five and are analogous to established RA pathotypes. 20 To facilitate the translation of these computationally derived pathotypes into routine clinical histopathological workflows, a diagnostic decision tree algorithm was subsequently developed.

text.text: Statistical analyses were performed using Python (v3.12).
Continuous variables were compared across clinical diagnoses and pathotypes using the Kruskal-Wallis or Mann-Whitney U test, as appropriate.
P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) method where stated.
Correlations between continuous digital pathology metrics and clinical disease activity scores were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation.
Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was utilised to evaluate the diagnostic utility of specific cellular markers in differentiating PsA from RA.
Categorical variables, including radiographic OA severity and longitudinal treatment responses, were visualised using stacked bar charts and cross-tabulations.
A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

text.text: To investigate histological overlap between clinical diagnoses, unsupervised clustering of the entire cohort (n=60) was performed utilising all seven histological markers.
Cluster number was evaluated via the elbow method and silhouette analysis, and three distinct phenotypic groups were defined.

Cluster 1 was characterised by high cellularity, vascularity, and CD3/CD20/CD68 expression; Cluster 2 by high vascularity alongside prominent CD138 and CD68 expression; and Cluster 3 by profound fibrosis.
Evaluating the diagnostic distribution across these profiles revealed that most seropositive RA patients mapped to the highly inflammatory Cluster 1, alongside 33% (n=7/21) of the PsA cohort.
Conversely, PsA patients comprised the largest proportion of Cluster 2 (50%, n=5/10), whereas Cluster 3 contained similar proportions of PsA, seropositive and seronegative RA patients.

Together, these data demonstrate that a subset of PsA patients share a highly inflamed, vascular, and lymphocyte/myeloidrich synovial phenotype with seropositive RA, whereas a distinct subset of PsA patients have synovial inflammation characterised by high CD138 expression (Supplementary Figures 10a-c).

text.text: To further dissect this inflammatory overlap, a secondary unsupervised clustering analysis was performed exclusively on patients categorised with a classic lymphomyeloid pathotype (n=37).
This sub-clustering yielded two distinct groups.

Cluster 1 exhibited traditional inflammatory hallmarks (higher CD3, CD20, CD68, vascularity, and overall cellularity), whereas Cluster 2 was distinguished by disproportionately high CD138 expression and fibrosis.

Diagnostic stratification of this sub-cohort revealed a clear divergence: 73% (n=11/15) of the lymphomyeloid seropositive RA patients localised to Cluster 1, accompanied by 40% (n=6/15) of the lymphomyeloid PsA patients.
By contrast, Cluster 2 was predominantly composed of PsA patients (50%, n=9/18) and only 22% (n=4/18) seropositive RA patients.

These findings indicate that while roughly half of lymphomyeloid PsA patients exhibit an inflammatory signature indistinguishable from seropositive RA, the remainder represent a distinct pathological subgroup driven by CD138 + plasma cell infiltration and stromal remodelling (Supplementary Figures 11a-c).

text.text: To deconstruct the heterogeneity of synovial inflammation specifically within the PsA cohort (n=22), unsupervised hierarchical clustering was performed utilising all seven histological markers.
This yielded three distinct phenotypic clusters, which were assigned descriptive labels based on their defining histological architecture.
Cluster 1, driven by high CD68 expression and dense overall cellularity, was designated the 'Dense Myeloid' pathotype.
Cluster 2, defined by profound fibrosis and a relative paucity of immune infiltration (low CD3, CD20, CD68, and CD138), was classified as the 'Fibro-Stromal' pathotype.
Finally, Cluster 3, distinguished by pronounced CD138 + plasma cell infiltration and increased vascularity, was named the 'Angio-Lymphoid' pathotype (Figures 5a and 5c, Supplementary Figures 12a-c).

text.text: We present the first computationally derived, PsA-specific synovial pathotypes.

By leveraging objective digital pathology to move beyond traditional RA-centric models, we defined three distinct pathotypes to characterise synovial inflammation in PsA: Dense Myeloid, Fibro-Stromal, and Angio-Lymphoid.

While a subset of PsA patients shares an inflammatory signature with seropositive RA, applying RA pathotypes to the broader PsA cohort fails to capture its unique fibrotic and plasmacell-driven architecture.
To bridge computational discovery and clinical utility, we translated these findings into a pragmatic, four-marker diagnostic decision tree to facilitate future tissue-driven studies in PsA.
A key biological insight is the prominent role of CD138 + plasma cells in the inflammatory PsA synovial microenvironment.

Unlike the CD20 + B cell-dominated RA lympho-myeloid pathotype, sub-clustering revealed a substantial subset of inflamed PsA characterised by disproportionate CD138 + plasma cell infiltration and hypervascularity.
This distinct Angio-Lymphoid signature justified substituting CD20 with CD138 in our PsA-specific algorithm.

This plasma cell enrichment aligns with previously published evidence of profound B-cell maturation in psoriatic disease, 8, 34, 42, 43 suggesting intra-articular terminal B-cell differentiation may be a defining feature of severe PsA synovitis.

text.text: Clinically, these pathotypes revealed a striking divergence between joint and skin phenotypes.

Synovial immune infiltration correlated inversely with cutaneous severity: patients with the pauci-immune Fibro-Stromal pathotype exhibited higher psoriasis BSA, whereas dense cellularity and CD138 expression correlated with lower BSA.

This divergence aligns with real-world observations where approximately 34% of PsA patients exhibit severe joint but mild skin involvement, 44 suggesting a tissue-specific compartmentalisation of the immune response.

text.text: Importantly, systematic radiographic evaluation confirmed the Fibro-Stromal signature is an intrinsic PsA feature, as concurrent knee osteoarthritis severity was distributed evenly across all pathotypes and decoupled from fibrosis.
Longitudinally, these pathotypes demonstrate potential to guide rational drug selection.
Following biopsy, patients predominantly initiated methotrexate or TNF inhibitors.

Fibro-Stromal patients trended towards higher subsequent treatment failure, where only 44% had a good or moderate response to treatment compared to 50% of the PsA patients with a Dense Myeloid pathotype and 80% of the PsA patients with a Angio-Lymphoid pathotype.

Although underpowered for statistical significance, this trend provides a compelling biological rationale: standard therapies may be sub-optimal for this skin-predominant, pauci-immune, and fibrotic phenotype.

Because IL-17 and IL-23 inhibitors demonstrate superior efficacy for skin clearance compared to TNF inhibition, 45, 46 the refractory nature of the Fibro-Stromal pathotype may reflect a mechanistic mismatch.

text.text: This highlights the need for a prospective study to explore the actionable opportunity to stratify these patients towards early IL-17/IL-23 inhibitor interventions, alongside an unmet need for novel therapeutics targeting pathogenic synovial fibroblasts.
Study limitations include the modest PsA cohort size (n=22), which constrained the statistical power of longitudinal analyses and necessitated grouping diverse drug classes.
Validation in larger, prospectively treated cohorts is required to confirm predictive values for specific biologics.

Additionally, while exclusively sampling the knee standardised the anatomical site and we rigorously excluded OA as a confounder, it remains unclear whether these pathotypes are uniformly represented in smaller joints.
Finally, our multi-modal histological framework is restricted to predefined markers.
Future studies leveraging single-cell and spatial transcriptomics 30, 31, 47-52 will be crucial.
Just as single-cell transcriptomics in RA discovered highly granular Cell-Type Abundance Phenotypes (CTAPs), 53 multi-omic technologies will inevitably refine these PsA pathotypes.

section.header: Implications of all the available evidence
Unsupervised Clustering for Novel Pathotype Discovery
Synovial tissue cohort and baseline histological characterisation
High-grade synovitis aligns with a lymphomyeloid pathotype in PsA and seropositive RA
Macrophage (CD68) expression differentiates PsA from seronegative RA
Vascularity and fibrosis are comparable across inflammatory arthritides
The pauci-immune pathotype is predominantly identified in patients receiving treatment
Synovial pathotypes and histological profiles are independent of disease duration
A subset of PsA patients shares the inflammatory synovial profile of seropositive RA
Unsupervised clustering defines three novel, clinically distinct synovial pathotypes in PsA
A clinically translatable decision tree algorithm for routine PsA synovial pathotyping
Longitudinal treatment outcomes and pathotype-specific therapeutic responses in PsA
Novel synovial pathotypes are independent of concurrent radiographic osteoarthritis
Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the manuscript preparation process
